faq.q: Why is sickle cell disease the top cause in African children?

faq.a: It is usually not an emergency, but persistent cases need embolisation to prevent long‑term problems.
Proceed with repeated aspiration and saline irrigation; consider surgical shunt if erection remains.

exam: What immediate steps do you take for a child with a 6‑hour painful erection? — Assess pain, obtain blood gas, start analgesia, aspirate corpora, consider phenylephrine.
How do you differentiate ischaemic from non‑ischaemic priapism at the bedside? — Pain severity, rigidity pattern, and blood gas results.
A child with known sickle cell disease presents with priapism; what systemic therapy should you add? — Aggressive hydration, oxygen, analgesia, and consider exchange transfusion if crisis severe.
Why is phenylephrine preferred over other vasoconstrictors? — It acts on α‑adrenergic receptors, rapidly reverses ischaemia with limited systemic effects when diluted.
What are the contraindications to phenylephrine in priapism? — Uncontrolled hypertension, severe cardiac disease; monitor blood pressure closely.
When is surgical shunting indicated? — When erection persists after aspiration and phenylephrine, typically >24 h or refractory to medical therapy.
How would you manage priapism if Doppler ultrasound is not available? — Rely on clinical assessment and blood gas; treat as ischaemic unless clear trauma suggests high‑flow.
What preventive advice do you give a child with SCD after an episode? — Stay well‑hydrated, avoid cold exposure, seek care within 4 h of erection, review medications.
ai.title: Priapism in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Priapism is a painful, prolonged erection lasting >4 h without sexual stimulation. In children it is most often ischaemic and linked to sickle cell disease, but other causes must be considered. Prompt recognition, staging and treatment prevent permanent erectile damage.

b: Ischaemic: painful, rigid shaft, flaccid glans, dark deoxygenated blood.
Non‑ischaemic: painless, partially rigid, bright red oxygenated blood.
sections.p: Priapism is an unwanted erection persisting >4 h, not related to sexual arousal. Diagnosis is clinical; differentiate ischaemic (low‑flow) from non‑ischaemic (high‑flow) by history and penile blood gas.

b: Stage I: <4 h, mild pain, corpora partially rigid.
Stage II: 4–24 h, severe pain, fully rigid.
Stage III: >24 h, necrosis risk, possible gangrene.
sections.p: Ischaemic priapism is staged by duration and corporal rigidity. Early (<4 h) has reversible tissue; >24 h risks fibrosis and permanent dysfunction.

b: Sickle cell disease – vaso‑occlusion of penile sinusoids.
Medications – trazodone, antipsychotics, antihypertensives.
Haemoglobinopathies – thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency.
Infections – malaria, HIV‑related vasculitis.
Trauma – perineal injury causing arterial‑venous fistula (high‑flow).
Herbal remedies – unknown vasodilators.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the leading cause in children is sickle cell disease (SCD). Other common aetiologies include medications, haematological disorders and perineal trauma.

b: Severe penile pain, especially with erection.
Rigid shaft, soft glans (ischaemic).
History of recent trauma (high‑flow).
sections.p: A child presents with a painful, rigid erection lasting several hours, often waking at night. No sexual stimulus is reported. In high‑flow cases the penis may be less tender and the glans remains soft.
Investigations aim to confirm type, identify cause and assess severity.

t.b: Distinguishes ischaemic from non‑ischaemic; low pO₂, high pCO₂, acidic pH = ischaemic.

t.a: CBC and sickle cell screen (Hb electrophoresis)
t.b: Detects SCD or other haemoglobinopathies; positive result points to vaso‑occlusive priapism.
Shows low flow in ischaemic, high arterial flow in non‑ischaemic; if unavailable, rely on clinical clues.
Identifies drug‑induced priapism; stop offending agent.

b: Erection >24 h.
Progressive loss of sensation.
Signs of infection or necrosis.
sections.p: Delayed treatment leads to corporal fibrosis, erectile dysfunction, and rarely penile gangrene.

b: Immediate analgesia and ice packs.
Corporal aspiration with saline irrigation.
Intracavernosal phenylephrine (avoid in hypertension, use dilute solution).
If aspiration fails, surgical shunt (e.g., Winter or Al‑Ghorab).
Treat SCD crisis with hydration, oxygen, analgesia, and exchange transfusion if severe.
Stop offending medications; replace with alternatives without priapism risk.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then relieve ischaemia urgently. Non‑ischaemic cases are observed or embolised if persistent.

b: Monthly review of sickle cell management plan.
Counsel on avoiding known triggers (certain drugs, alcohol).
Arrange urology follow‑up after any episode.
sections.p: Children with SCD need education on early presentation and hydration. Review medication lists regularly.

b: Cellulitis – swelling, erythema, systemic signs, not rigid.
Perineal abscess – localized pain, fluctuance, fever.
Neurogenic erection – associated spinal injury, not painful.
sections.p: Conditions that may mimic priapism include penile cellulitis, perineal abscess, and erectile dysfunction from neurological injury.

b: Partial arterial flow can appear normal on bedside Doppler; rely on clinical rigidity.
Normal CBC does not exclude SCD; confirm with electrophoresis.
sections.p: Blood gas may be borderline in early ischaemia; Doppler may be unavailable, leading to misclassification.

whenToSeekHelp: Increasing pain or loss of sensation
Signs of infection, fever, or necrosis
